source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: First n-back test of an LLM. gpt-3.5-turbo accuracy and d-prime fall as n rises from 1 to 3, as in humans. Authors call the limit human-like (about n=3) and propose n-back as an LLM working-memory benchmark.
numbers: Verbal and spatial n-back, n=1,2,3, temperature 1. Metric d-prime; capacity defined as the n where d-prime drops to about 1. Kruskal-Wallis and Wilcoxon tests used.
limits: Text-only n-back with prompted 'm' / '-' answers. Later work (Hu and Lewis 2024, Gong and Zhang 2024) shows part of the drop is task misunderstanding or attention dilution, not a fixed store.
agent_relevance: Capacity-style limits show up in a 2023 chat model. A scaffold should not rely on the model holding more than a few updated items without writing them out.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Extra load changes capacity as in human WM work. Noise symbols (distractors) and abstract-reasoning variants of spatial n-back lowered capacity; larger grids (3x3 up to 7x7) raised it, probably from less interference between trials.
numbers: Grid sizes 3x3, 4x4, 5x5, 7x7; variants: noise, feedback, chain-of-thought, two abstract row/column match types. Exact d-prime values only in figures.
limits: Grid-size effect has no human data; authors say it needs human replication.
agent_relevance: Interference between similar items hurts; keep items distinct in the working notes.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Feedback and chain-of-thought prompts helped but did not remove the decline with n.
numbers: Feedback line: 'Feedback: your last response was correct/wrong'. CoT: 'Let's think step by step' added.
quote: the trend of performance declines and the capacity limit still bear a striking resemblance to humans
limits: Gains are small versus the effect of n; authors say the trend and limit remain.
agent_relevance: Step-by-step text helps only partly; prompt wording alone does not lift the limit.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Model comparison on verbal n-back: GPT-4 far exceeds GPT-3.5; seven smaller open models (Bloomz-7B, Bloomz-7B1-mt, ChatGLM-6B v1.0 and v1.1, Vicuna-7B and 13B) have very low capacity and are nearly indistinguishable.
numbers: 8 LLMs total; GPT-4 tested only to n=3 for cost.
limits: Few models; no human sample run by the authors (human curve taken from literature).
agent_relevance: WM-style capacity tracks overall model strength, as in the human WM and Gf link, but only as a correlation across models.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
finding: Small decoder-only transformers trained from scratch on N-back lose accuracy as N rises. Attention to position i-N grows with accuracy, and total attention entropy rises with N, so attention gets diluted.
numbers: 24-letter inputs; layers L in {1,2}, heads H in {1,2,4}; extended to N=6 where test accuracy falls roughly logarithmically; larger L or H often above 95% at all N with slight decline.
limits: Toy models, not pretrained LLMs; authors say direct comparison with LLMs is not straightforward.
agent_relevance: A mechanism for a capacity limit: more items to bind means diffuse attention. Fewer, sharper retrieval targets per step should reduce errors.

source: Hu and Lewis (2024) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them?
finding: Poor n-back is partly a task-understanding failure. Weak models answer a 1-back task when told 2- or 3-back. Strong models do not.
numbers: 8 models, 50 trials per n, 24-letter sequences with 8 matches. Retrieval accuracy at 2-back/3-back: Qwen1.5-14b 0.09/0.08; Llama3.1-8b 0.14/0.17; Gemma2-27b 0.57/0.36; GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.51/0.43; Qwen2-72b 0.81/0.84; Llama3.1-70b 0.99/0.93. 1-back is 1.00 for all.
limits: Better prompts might change comprehension; no circuit-level test. Llama attention more diffuse than Qwen, unexplained. Read through a summarising fetch of the ar5iv page.
agent_relevance: Before blaming capacity, check the model is doing the stated task. A code check of the rule actually applied is cheap.

source: Hu and Lewis (2024) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them?
finding: Llama-3.1-70B holds up to n=10 with retrieval accuracy falling smoothly. An in-context curriculum (demonstrations from 1-back up to n-back) lifts large-n scores.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B retrieval at n=8,9,10: 75.25%, 66.08%, 57.1%. With curriculum: 79.83%, 80.17%, 71.67%. Task accuracy at n=8,9,10: 83.33, 78.25, 71.92, rising to 90.08, 90.08, 84.75 with curriculum.
limits: One model for the extended range.
agent_relevance: Worked examples ordered from easy to hard are a cheap scaffold that measurably raised a WM-style task.

source: Hu and Lewis (2024) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them?
finding: Task-set drift: Gemma-2-27B drifts toward 1-back answers over a long dialogue, and earlier 1-back errors speed the drift. Interactive demonstrations helped little.
numbers: Interactive demos: Llama-3.1-70B 2-back 0.99 (no change), 3-back 0.62 (down 0.31); Gemma-2-27B 2-back 0.61 (+0.04), 3-back 0.31 (-0.05). Max mean retrieval attention: Qwen2-72b 71.98%, Qwen1.5-14b 38.95%, Llama3.1-70b 8.52%, Llama3.1-8b 4.86%.
limits: Attention pattern differs by family, not explained.
agent_relevance: Errors feed on earlier errors in the same context. Restate the rule each step and avoid showing the model its own faulty outputs.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working Memory Identifies Reasoning Limits in Language Models
finding: N-back d-prime across the InstructGPT line up to GPT-4 shows a U-shaped curve with scale. Larger models have more WM but still do not match humans consistently, more so as tasks get harder.
numbers: 7 models: text-ada-001, babbage-001, curie-001, davinci-001, davinci-002, gpt-3.5-turbo-0613, gpt-4-0613; verbal and spatial n-back; d-prime = Z(hit) - Z(false alarm). Smallest model alternates 'm' and '-' and copies the QA format.
limits: Authors admit n-back is not a pure WM measure (cite Jaeggi 2010). Mostly closed GPT models. Exact d-prime values only in figures.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a bigger model removes the limit; use an external store for many items.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working Memory Identifies Reasoning Limits in Language Models
finding: Fancier prompts hurt small models. Answer-only beat AutoCoT, plan-and-solve and tree-of-thought for small LMs on BIG-Bench Hard; for text-davinci-002, writing the reasoning as code helped.
numbers: BBH, 23 tasks; prompts AO, CoT, SC-CoT, PS, ToT, AutoCoT, plus the authors' CoT+. Tracking Shuffled Objects was the clearest failure: models lose which ball belongs to whom.
limits: Per-task numbers are in figures; no single percent in the extracted text. CoT+ was built from error analysis on the same tasks, so it may be tuned to them.
agent_relevance: Match scaffold complexity to model strength. Weak or cheap models need simple steps.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working Memory Identifies Reasoning Limits in Language Models
finding: Cognitive strategies from human n-back players, moved into prompts as CoT+: rehearsal (restate the facts so far), chunking (group items per person), and a focus cue. Rehearsal in a counting task used the trigger 'so before that'.
numbers: Strategies came from interviews with human participants (App. E.3). Unrelated context number: BBH zero-shot CoT Llama 3 70B 50.1 vs 81.3 with 3 shots; Llama 3 8B 28.6 vs 61.1.
limits: No exact CoT+ gain in the extracted text. The Llama figures are about shots, not CoT+.
agent_relevance: A ready template for a state that rehearses and chunks the live facts before each step.

source: Huang, Sun, Wang, Dredze (2025) Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory
finding: Models cannot privately commit to a hidden value. In Number Guessing (pick 1-10, probe each i, 200 times) the 'yes' probabilities should sum to 1. Most models sum to 0.
numbers: 17 models. Sum 0: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o-2024-05-13, GPT-4o-2024-11-20, GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V3. Near 1: GPT-4o-2024-08-06 1.085, Llama-3.1-8B 0.980, Llama-3.1-405B 1.195. When saying yes they favored seven.
limits: Output-only inference of latent state; the 'architectural deficiency' claim has no ablation.
agent_relevance: Anything the agent must keep hidden or fixed across steps has to be written down; it cannot live in the model between calls.

source: Huang, Sun, Wang, Dredze (2025) Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory
finding: Yes-No Deduction (20-questions style, up to 250 answers) shows self-contradiction in long chains.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini failed 200 of 200 trials; GPT-4o-2024-08-06 failed 173 of 200. Failures peaked at 20-30 questions (mini) and 30-40 (GPT-4o). Hint plus object specified cut failures only to 145.
limits: Single snapshots; prompt-sensitive.
agent_relevance: A code check of the answer log for contradictions would catch these.

source: Huang, Sun, Wang, Dredze (2025) Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory
finding: Math Magic (multi-step manipulation of four numbers; final two must match): written reasoning turns a near-zero task into a high-score task, so the work sits in the tokens, not a latent state.
numbers: 150 trials per model. Without CoT: GPT-4o-mini 0%, GPT-4o-2024-08-06 2.0%, Llama-3.1-405B 26.0%. With CoT or reasoning models: DeepSeek-R1 100%, o3-mini 96.7%, QwQ-32B 90.0%, o1-mini 50.0%, o4-mini 36.0%, GPT-4o-2024-08-06 20.7%, GPT-4o-mini 3.3%.
limits: Prompt-specific; GPT-4.1 not scored (said inputs were missing); original Kaprekar variant dropped for contamination.
agent_relevance: Strong support for an external, written working memory: externalise each intermediate state.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: An Empirical Study of Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: They reproduce Gong's n-back drop, but on simple and complex spans LLMs meet or exceed human norms. Storage is not the weak point; reversal is.
numbers: Forward digit span at d=50: 0.99-1.00 for all six models (humans about 7 digits). Backward span at d=15: Gemma-2-9B 0.21, Gemma-2-27B 0.59, Llama-3.1-8B 0.18, Llama-3.1-70B 0.83, Qwen2-7B 0.00, Qwen2-72B 0.51. Operation span 0.93-0.99; reading span 0.66-0.98. n-back 1/2/3 for Llama-3.1-70B 0.93/0.82/0.82 vs human about 0.98/0.91/0.75.
limits: Open models 7B-72B only; human numbers are rough norms.
agent_relevance: Plain storage of a long rule list is fine; the weak step is manipulating or updating it.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: An Empirical Study of Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: Parameter count correlates with mean span performance; attention-head count correlates less. Reversal and concurrent processing cut recall (complex spans).
numbers: Parameters vs mean span r=0.82, p<0.05; attention heads r=0.76, p=0.08.
limits: Six models, so low power.
agent_relevance: Capacity grows with scale; the manipulation burden is what causes errors.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: An Empirical Study of Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: Larger span scores did not carry over to other executive tasks or problem-solving benchmarks. On the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test all LLMs fall below human accuracy and cannot hold the rule after feedback.
numbers: WCST: 3060 trials per model (102 trials x 30 prompts). Text says human accuracy is typically 70-80%; model accuracies in the table range 0.29 (Llama-3.1-8B) to about 0.53. Accuracy sharply drops after a brief rise, read as forgetting the rule.
limits: Prompt had to spell out an exact strategy because human-style instructions failed in pilots. The extracted table has two garbled rows, so only the Llama and Qwen rows are quoted.
agent_relevance: The Kyllonen-Christal logic (WM predicts reasoning) did not hold across models here. Capacity alone is not the agent's bottleneck; control is.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: An Empirical Study of Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: Flanker task: incongruent trials sharply hurt LLMs. A reasoning model fixes most of it.
numbers: Incongruent accuracy 40-60% vs human 93-96%. Llama-3.1-8B congruent 0.944, incongruent 0.471; with reasoning 0.977 and 0.910. Qwen2-32B 0.917/0.638 base; 0.994/0.985 with reasoning.
limits: Reasoning variants are DeepSeek-R1 distilled; high token cost.
agent_relevance: Distractor suppression is a weakness; a step that lists only the relevant facts and drops the rest should help.

source: Jaroslawicz et al. (2025) How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once? (IFScale)
finding: Rule load test: up to 500 keyword rules in a business-report task. Even the best models reach only 68% at 500. Three decay shapes: threshold (o3, gemini-2.5-pro), linear (gpt-4.1, claude-sonnet-4), exponential (gpt-4o, llama-4-scout).
numbers: 20 models, 7 providers, 5 seeds per density. At 500 rules: grok-3 61.9%, o3 62.8%, qwen3 26.9%. Reasoning models stay near-perfect to about 100-250 rules (top two to 150 or more).
limits: Keyword inclusion is easy per rule, so it isolates load. No human baseline.
agent_relevance: Direct match to 'limits on holding many rules': cap active rules per step and split big rule sets over steps.

source: Jaroslawicz et al. (2025) How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once? (IFScale)
finding: Rules placed early are satisfied more. This primacy effect peaks near 150-200 rules, then fades toward uniform failure above 300.
numbers: Primacy ratio (error in last third / error in first third) converges to about 1.0-1.5 at 300+ rules. Reasoning-model latency: one model 12.4 s at 10 rules to 436 s at 250; o3 26.3 s to 219.6 s.
limits: Single task type.
agent_relevance: Put the most important rules first, but do not count on it at high load.

source: Jaroslawicz et al. (2025) How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once? (IFScale)
finding: Error type shifts under load from modification to omission. The top reasoning models o3 and o4-mini cut output length and coherence rather than fail rule by rule.
numbers: At 500 rules o3 emits about 1,500 tokens; o3 and o4-mini fall below the coherence score of 6 that defines a plausible report.
limits: Grader-based coherence score.
agent_relevance: Check by code that every rule got a verdict; silent omission is the main failure.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Text Raven-style Digit Matrices: text-davinci-003 beat the average of 40 UCLA undergraduates zero-shot, with a difficulty pattern like humans. More distinct rules means harder, for both.
numbers: Humans N=40. GPT-3 vs humans, generative answers: OR=1.88 (95% CI 1.21-2.91), p=0.005; multiple choice OR=6.27 (CI 3.28-11.99). Item-pattern correlation r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Number of unique rules: humans OR=0.61, p=0.0047; progression rules harder: humans OR=0.41, p=0.0001.
limits: Items are new in form but rule types may echo training data. Later work (Gendron; Camposampiero) finds weaker results. No WM account in the paper.
agent_relevance: Rule count drives difficulty in both humans and models, matching a load view of Gf. Keep rules per step low.

source: Gendron et al. (2023) Large Language Models Are Not Strong Abstract Reasoners
finding: Across abstract-reasoning sets including a text Raven (RAVENT), open-answer accuracy is low. Chain-of-thought did not raise results overall.
numbers: RAVENT open QA text/symbolic: text-davinci-003 0.343/0.234; GPT-3.5-turbo 0.226/0.161; GPT-4 0.410/0.330; LLaMA-7B 0.000/0.000. RAVENT multiple choice text/symbolic: text-davinci-003 0.452 (text), GPT-4 0.697/0.535. Text states CoT results are not higher than base models.
limits: Authors suspect Raven items leaked into GPT-4 training. Fine-tuned LLaMA2 failed to generalise out of distribution. Table column labels were not fully clear in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: A strong score on a famous Gf test may be memory of the test; check the agent on fresh items.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty?
finding: Reasoning models collapse on longer Raven-style matrices with wider value ranges and noise, despite more thinking tokens.
numbers: o3-mini: 86.6% on I-RAVEN to 17.0% on I-RAVEN-X with uncertainty, using 3.4 times more reasoning tokens. DeepSeek R1: 80.6% to 23.2%. Neuro-symbolic ARLC: 98.6% to 88.0%.
limits: Symbolic rendering of RAVEN; perception noise is simulated.
agent_relevance: A fixed-code solver beats the model at rule execution. Do rule applying in code; use the model to propose rules.

source: Kim and Schuster (2023) Entity Tracking in Language Models
finding: State tracking under many operations (boxes and objects): only GPT-3.5 models pretrained on code tracked state; text-only GPT-3 and Flan-T5 did not beat a copy-the-initial-state shortcut.
numbers: In the Alchemy set the initial state alone gives 62.7% accuracy on unchanged boxes, but a probing classifier gets only 3.1% on the changed ones. Fine-tuned T5 generalises partly to new entities and longer operation sequences, falling on harder splits.
limits: Exact in-context accuracy per operation count is in a figure only.
agent_relevance: Code-trained models track state better; keep state as a structured variable updated by code.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?
finding: Long-context tasks including multi-hop variable tracking show big drops with length. Only about half the models claiming 32K or more keep quality at 32K.
numbers: Average score 4K to 128K: GPT-4 effective 64K (96.6 at 4K, 81.2 at 128K); Llama3.1-70B 64K (96.5 to 66.6); Qwen2-72B 32K; Mixtral-8x22B 31.7 at 128K; DBRX 2.4 at 64K.
limits: Variable tracking is one of 13 tasks; the table is the all-task average.
agent_relevance: Holding things in context is not holding them in mind; keep the live set short.

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models
finding: Psychometric test of LLMs: scores across 12 tests correlate (positive manifold) and give a general ability factor; parameters correlate with it with diminishing returns.
numbers: 591 LLMs, 12 tests mapped to Gf, Gkn, Grw, Gq; a combined Gkn/Grw group factor was found.
limits: No WM measures in the battery; achievement versus intelligence left open. Only the front pages were read.
agent_relevance: A general factor suggests one scaffold gain may carry across tasks, but it says nothing about capacity itself.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Agent design with an explicit working memory: a data structure persisting across LLM calls. Each call builds its prompt from a subset and parses output back into variables. It follows Soar and Baddeley-Hitch, and treats chain-of-thought as the LLM context acting as WM.
numbers: Framework only; no accuracy numbers. Memory types: working, episodic, semantic, procedural.
quote: it is a data structure that persists across LLM calls
limits: Survey and proposal, not a test of capacity benefits.
agent_relevance: This is the shape of our design: the program holds the working state and passes the model only the slice it needs.
